question: Can Bayesian inference jointly learn neural-network weights and an unbounded posterior over depth without choosing a maximum architecture in advance?

key_findings.claim: The UDN is a conventional shared-prefix neural network coupled to an unbounded latent truncation, rather than a continuous-depth or fixed-point limit.
key_findings.evidence: An infinite sequence of independently parameterized layers produces hidden states; an output head can attach at every layer; a positive-integer truncation selects which head generates each response. Different depths share all prefix weights.

key_findings.claim: A finite-support variational member can still explore arbitrary depths because the family, not each member, is unbounded.
key_findings.evidence: The truncation family requires every individual q to have bounded support, while some continuously parameterized member can place its mode at every positive integer. A truncated-Poisson construction and nested q(theta|ell) reduce the ELBO to a finite sum over currently active layers.

anchors.section: Truncated Poisson family and finite ELBO

key_findings.claim: Dynamic variational inference grows or prunes active layer parameters as gradient optimization moves the truncation posterior.
key_findings.evidence: Before each ELBO evaluation, a dynamic computation graph instantiates only weights within the current support of q(ell) and removes inactive free variational parameters. No external architecture proposal or split-merge heuristic selects depth.

key_findings.claim: On synthetic spirals the learned posterior becomes deeper with increasing label complexity and improves average accuracy.
key_findings.evidence: Across rotation speeds, UDN average test accuracy is 91.7±1.1%, versus 90.5±0.7 for DUN-10 and 84.8-89.3 for selected fixed depths. At near-random high rotation, independent runs select different depths, appropriately exposing non-identifiability rather than a stable optimum.

key_findings.claim: On CIFAR-10 UDN modestly beats tested finite and implicit-depth baselines while adapting depth to task difficulty.
key_findings.evidence: UDN with ResNet reaches 94.4±0.2%, versus 94.0±0.2 for the strongest displayed finite ResNets and 93.8±0.3 for MDEQ. Posterior depths are shallow for deer-vs-car, deeper for cat-vs-dog, and broad/deep for the full ten-class task.

method.core_idea: Turn network depth into a positive-integer latent variable and design an approximate-posterior family that is computationally finite at every iterate but can move to any finite depth.
method.mechanism: Place priors on an infinite sequence of layer weights and Poisson-like truncation; factor q(theta,ell) into a truncated-Poisson q(ell) and nested weight posterior matching the prior beyond ell; evaluate a finite ELBO; use dynamic automatic-differentiation graphs to add or remove layer variational parameters as q's support changes.
assumptions: A shared-prefix family makes predictions at different depths comparable.
The chosen weight and truncation priors express useful complexity preferences.
A truncated-Poisson variational posterior adequately approximates the true depth posterior.
Gradient optimization can navigate depth modes without getting trapped by transient support changes.
Dataset complexity is usefully reflected by predictive depth.

techniques.role: Defines a posterior over where an infinite shared-prefix network emits output.
Makes each variational expectation finite while retaining arbitrary depth reachability.
Matches unused deep weights to their prior so only active prefixes contribute to KL.
Creates and removes free variational layer parameters during optimization.
Tests whether inferred depth changes with controlled task difficulty.

evaluations.setting: Two-branch spiral datasets with increasing rotation speed
evaluations.metric: Test accuracy and posterior mean depth
evaluations.result: UDN achieves 91.7±1.1% average and generally deepens with complexity
94.4±0.2%, above displayed finite, NODE/ANODE, and MDEQ baselines

evaluations.setting: Easy deer-car versus hard cat-dog subsets
evaluations.result: Easy pair uses a few layers; harder and full tasks use deeper supports

evaluations.setting: Independent runs on nearly random spiral labels
evaluations.result: Depth varies across runs when no clear predictive structure remains

limitations: The posterior approximation has a restricted truncated-Poisson shape and is not shown to capture multimodal depth uncertainty.
All depths share prefix weights and output-head design, so this is depth search within one generator rather than arbitrary architecture search.
Training an ensemble-like collection of heads and weight posteriors can be more expensive than the eventual chosen finite network.
CIFAR-10 experiments are modest-scale, with no ImageNet, language-model, transformer, or modern NAS comparison.
Reported gains over strong finite models are small and use architecture/hyperparameter choices from the study.
Bayesian prior sensitivity and calibration under distribution shift are not deeply evaluated.
failure_modes: Early posterior mass at shallow depth prevents useful deeper layers from receiving training signal.
A broad or multimodal true depth posterior is forced into one truncated-Poisson region.
Shared prefix weights create interference among shallow and deep predictors.
Dynamic optimizer state becomes stale or inconsistent when parameters enter and leave support.
A weak prior rewards unnecessary growth or over-penalizes complex tasks.
Depth adapts to label noise rather than meaningful compositional complexity.
reusable_insights: Distinguish an unbounded variational family from computationally infinite individual distributions.
Match inactive latent variables to the prior so an infinite model yields a finite objective.
Use controlled difficulty sweeps to validate that inferred complexity changes for the intended reason.
Report posterior instability when the task has no identifiable best complexity.
Compare adaptive models with compute-matched finite baselines, not only fixed small architectures.
open_questions: Can richer variational families represent multiple plausible depth modes while remaining dynamically finite?
How does posterior depth behave in transformers and large-scale language modeling?
Can amortized or continual inference reuse learned depth distributions across tasks?
What prior yields consistent depth recovery and robust calibration?
How should compute, memory, and uncertainty gains be compared with pruning and one-shot NAS?

competitive_landscape.title: Depth Uncertainty in Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: DUN marginalizes predictions over shared subnetworks up to a user-specified maximum with single-pass inference. UDN removes that maximum and dynamically grows the active posterior support, at greater inference/training complexity.

competitive_landscape.title: Variational Depth Search in ResNets
competitive_landscape.difference: Variational Depth Search infers a posterior over depths within a fixed maximum ResNet and prunes from that supernet. UDN defines an unbounded generative model and creates deeper parameters when demanded by the optimized posterior.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Networks with Stochastic Depth
competitive_landscape.difference: Stochastic Depth drops residual blocks during training but deploys a predetermined deep network. UDN treats output depth as a Bayesian latent variable and marginalizes its posterior rather than using dropout as regularization.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Ordinary Differential Equations
competitive_landscape.difference: Neural ODEs tie depth to integration time in a continuous vector field. UDN retains ordinary discrete layers with separate weights and learns a posterior over finite truncations of an infinite sequence.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: UDN is an infinitely deep probabilistic neural network with genuinely unbounded depth inference driven solely by variational optimization.
novelty_assessment.evidence: A new bounded-member/unbounded-family construction, finite ELBO, dynamic implementation, controlled complexity experiments, and CIFAR comparisons demonstrate the mechanism.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The variational construction is a clean Bayesian-nonparametric extension of depth uncertainty. Empirical evidence supports adaptive growth, but scale, posterior-family sensitivity, and compute-adjusted advantages remain open.

reviewer_notes: Read all 15 extracted pages, including the variational derivation, dynamic algorithm, experimental appendices, and discussion. Four primary arXiv competitors were checked on 2026-08-23. I did not independently reproduce the ELBO gradients or training runs.
